title: 1970 VW Transporter Double Cab Pickup Is a Lovable Bargain

body_markdown:
There are few classics more lovable and more practical than the Volkswagen Transporter, also known as the Type 2 or, simply, the Bus. This recently refreshed example from 1970 is more practical than most, with its combination of double cab up front and a pickup bed in the back. The price makes it easy to love, too. This pickup sold Wednesday[on Bring a Trailer](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1970-volkswagen-transporter-double-cab-pickup/) for just over $20K.


Those familiar with Volkswagen Transporters will recognize this as a second-generation (1967–79, or T2) example. The visual giveaways are the one-piece windshield and the lack of a chrome “V” on the Bus’s face. As those visual changes suggest, the second gen was more of an evolution than a revolution compared to the first (produced from 1950 to 1967 in Germany). There were notable mechanical improvements, however. The second-gen Transporter’s rear suspension ditched the swing-axle setup of the first-gen in favor of half-shafts and constant-velocity joints. VW ensured that the air-cooled, 1.6-liter flat-four in the rear made “a little more hp and a lot more torque” than the original engine: 57 hp at 4400 rpm and 81 lb-ft of torque at 3000 rpm. The fuel tank was also bigger, with a capacity of 16 gallons rather than 10.6.

This double-cab pickup belonged to VW’s 1970 commercial line. It was, in fact, called a “Truck,” advertised alongside the panel van, Kombi, and single-cab pickup. What we recognize as the “Bus” was marketed to non-business customers as a VW Wagon. The non-commercial variants included the station wagon, the Kombi (again), and the Campmobile. The Double Cab was aimed at people who wanted the enclosed passenger compartment of the Kombi with the “unencumbered flatbed” of the pickup. “You might think of it as our open and shut case,” chirped the brochure.


Bring a Trailer / bcallen87


The Double Cab’s bed is shorter than that of the regular pickup, measuring 73.0 inches long and 61.8 inches wide and fitted with the same wooden runners to make it easy to slide equipment or cargo into or out of the vehicle. Gross weight rating was the same across all commercial variants (4795 pounds). The Double Cab’s payload rating, without the optional bows or tarpaulin, was 2260 pounds.


Bring a Trailer / bcallen87


Sharp eyes will spot that our featured Transporter does not wear Neptune Blue, the single shade of blue available for 1970 “Trucks.” Indeed, the VW Classic Parts certificate that comes with the vehicle notes that this U.S. market example was originally painted Lotus White and fitted with a Dark Beige leatherette interior. It was refurbished between 2014 and 2016, when its owner repainted it in the two-tone blue-and-white it wears today. Along the way, they also replaced some body panels (we’re not sure which ones) and did some rust repair. They installed bucket seats up front from a Porsche 911 (hilarious) and added Dynamat to the interior—a welcome upgrade, because if you’ve ever driven a Transporter, you’ll know that they have all the noise suppression of a tin can. That same owner replaced a right-side axle shaft and gave the flat-four (which already boasted electronic ignition) a valve adjustment and a new starter before selling it went to Bring a Trailer in[2021](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1970-volkswagen-1970-vw-bus-type-2-double-cab/) , when it was bid to $25,250 but failed to meet reserve.


The engine has received more love since; the most recent seller notes that they withdrew the pickup from a Mecum auction in Arizona earlier this year because the engine “was not running correctly.” The carburetor has since been rebuilt, and the fuel lines have been replaced, along with the fuel filter and spark plugs.

While one of the wheels is beginning to rust, and there’s another problem spot near a bed-side hinge, this pickup looks fresh for a vehicle from 1970, in large part thanks to that recent paint job. At $20,213 (including buyer’s premium), someone got a bargain on this Bus; a regular Kombi van is worth[$21,500](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/volkswagen/transporter_(van)/1970/1970-volkswagen-transporter_(van)-kombi?id=aCn1I000000CwksSAC) in #3 (good) condition in the Hagerty Price Guide. The double-cab bodystyle makes this one slightly unusual, and the two-tone paint sets it off beautifully.


Just 20 grand for a vehicle that is as charming as it is practical? It’s a reminder that you shouldn’t be scared off Transporters by the eye-watering prices of the first-gen, many-windowed variants. There’s much more to the vintage VW Bus story, and you needn’t spend six figures—or anywhere close—to enjoy the air-cooled, vintage-van life. Just remember to go slow, because these bad boys top out at 65 mph.
